findings.draft_passage: I looked at Miss Baker, wondering what it was she "got done."
findings.source_has: Her host looked at her incredulously. "You are!" He took down his drink as if it were a drop in the bottom of a glass. "How you ever get anything done is beyond me." I looked at Miss Baker, wondering what it was she "got done."
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: the scare-quoted phrase 'got done' reads as an echo of something just said, but no one in the draft has said anything about getting things done — the triggering exchange between Tom and Miss Baker was cut, leaving the quoted phrase without an antecedent utterance and Nick's wondering unmotivated.

findings.draft_passage:
"Well, he told me once he was an Oxford man."
"I don't believe it."
"Why not?"
"I don't know," she insisted, "I just don't think he went there."
findings.source_has: In the source Jordan says 'However, I don't believe it' — Jordan is the doubter throughout. Nick asks 'Why not?' and Jordan replies 'I don't know, I just don't think he went there.' The draft moves the disbelief to Nick's mouth, then immediately has Jordan also deny it ('she insisted… I just don't think he went there'), making Jordan contradict her own prior statement ('he told me once he was an Oxford man') within two lines.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: Jordan reports Gatsby's Oxford claim, Nick apparently disbelieves it, then Jordan is said to 'insist' she also doesn't believe it — Jordan appears to contradict herself in consecutive sentences, which is incoherent without knowing the source reassigned the scepticism entirely to Jordan from the start.

findings.draft_passage:
"Well, he told me once he was an Oxford man."
"I don't believe it."
"Why not?"
"I don't know," she insisted, "I just don't think he went there."
findings.source_has: Jordan says 'Well, he told me once he was an Oxford man.' Nick asks 'Why not?' only after Jordan herself says 'However, I don't believe it.' In the source Jordan is the skeptic; the draft reassigns 'I don't believe it' to Nick, inverting who doubts Gatsby's Oxford claim.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely misled: the draft makes Nick the doubter and Jordan the uncertain defender, whereas the source makes Jordan the doubter and Nick the curious questioner — a meaningful reversal of which character distrusts Gatsby's story.

findings.draft_passage: "But I like across the street better! Hot and small—yes, but full of memories."
findings.source_has: Wolfshiem says 'But I like across the street better!' then Gatsby interjects 'It's too hot over there,' and only then Wolfshiem concedes 'Hot and small—yes, but full of memories.' The 'yes' is a direct reply to Gatsby's objection.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: Wolfshiem volunteers that the rival restaurant is 'hot and small' and immediately concedes the point with 'yes' — appearing to argue with himself — because Gatsby's intervening objection, which the concession answers, has been cut.

findings.draft_passage: I walked out the back way—just as Gatsby had when he had made his nervous circuit of the house half an hour before
findings.source_has: Source establishes Gatsby's nervous pre-arrival circuit outside Nick's house before Daisy came; draft omits this entirely, leaving the back-reference to 'his nervous circuit of the house' without antecedent in the draft.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader of the draft alone has seen no circuit by Gatsby; they are genuinely confused by a comparative reference to an action that, in the draft, never happened.

findings.draft_passage: "Did you notice Daisy's face when that girl asked her to put her under a cold shower?"
findings.source_has: Source contains the full Miss Baedeker tipsy-table scene in which a girl's head is stuck in the pool and a cold shower is suggested; the draft cuts this entire exchange, leaving Tom's reference to 'that girl' and 'a cold shower' with no antecedent anywhere in the draft.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader of the draft is genuinely confused: no girl, no pool incident, and no cold-shower suggestion appear anywhere in the draft, so Tom's question is completely opaque rather than merely less decorated.

findings.draft_passage: the other three mounted and rode away. "My God, I believe the man's coming," said Tom on the porch.
findings.source_has: In the source Tom speaks before the group departs—while Gatsby is still inside fetching his hat and the others are about to mount. The draft's compression places Tom's line after stating all three (including Tom) rode away, making Tom simultaneously departed and present on the porch.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: the draft has just said Tom rode away with the others, yet Tom is immediately quoted speaking on the porch—an irreconcilable contradiction, not a mere stylistic reduction.

findings.draft_passage: "About Gatsby," he corrected himself when Jordan laughed at "medium."
findings.source_has: Jordan asks "Do you mean you've been to a medium?" Tom is confused and laughs before clarifying "About Gatsby!" — the word 'medium' is introduced by Jordan's question, which the draft cut entirely.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: Tom 'corrects himself' for apparently having used the word 'medium,' but no such remark appears anywhere in the draft, and Jordan has not laughed at anything; the referent of the correction is missing, not merely less ornamented.

findings.draft_passage: He drew me into his office in a reverent voice and offered me a cigar.
findings.source_has: He drew me into his office, remarking in a reverent voice that it was a sad time for all of us, and offered me a cigar.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: 'in a reverent voice' cannot modify 'drew me into his office' (drawing is not a vocal act), so the sentence has no coherent predicate for that adverbial phrase — the clause it originally modified ('remarking … that it was a sad time for all of us') was cut, leaving a dangling modifier that makes the sentence non-parseable as written.

findings.draft_passage: "Go on! Why, my God! they used to go there by the hundreds."
findings.source_has: Owl-eyes spoke to me by the gate. 'I couldn't get to the house,' he remarked. 'Neither could anybody else.' 'Go on!' He started. 'Why, my God! they used to go there by the hundreds.'
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: 'Go on!' is a surprised rebuttal to Nick's line 'Neither could anybody else,' which was cut from the draft; without that trigger, the exclamation has no referent and reads as an unmotivated non-sequitur rather than a response in a two-line exchange.
